extra.message: response.set_cookie('portal_crumb', marker) sets a cookie reflecting user input without HttpOnly or Secure flags (Django defaults httonly=False, secure=False). The cookie is readable by JavaScript and transmittable over cleartext HTTP.

urllib.request.urlopen(endpoint, timeout=3) fetches a URL taken directly from request.GET['endpoint'] with no scheme/host allow-listing. This enables server-side requests to internal services, cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254), and arbitrary external hosts.
The verifier PINs {'north': '4812', 'south': '5930'} are hardcoded in source and used to authenticate requests on lines 116-119. Hardcoded credentials are discoverable and cannot be rotated per user.

Access-Control-Allow-Origin is set to the reflected request Origin header and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is set to 'true' (line 128). This permits any origin to make credentialed cross-origin requests and read the responses, bypassing the same-origin policy.

extra.message: The response explicitly disables browser protections: X-XSS-Protection is set to '0' (line 135) and Content-Security-Policy is set to an empty string (line 136). This removes reflected-XSS mitigations and CSP enforcement for the response.

extra.message: SECRET_KEY falls back to the hardcoded value 'dev-only-change-me' when DJANGO_SECRET_KEY is unset. If deployed without the env var, the Django secret key is a publicly known constant, enabling session forgery, signed-cookie tampering, and CSRF token forgery.

DEBUG defaults to True (os.environ.get('DJANGO_DEBUG', '1') == '1'). If the env var is unset in deployment, Django runs in debug mode, exposing detailed error pages with stack traces, settings, and environment variables to attackers.

extra.message: The default database URL contains hardcoded credentials (postgres:postgres). When DATABASE_URL is not set, the application connects with these known credentials.

user.set_password('ChangeMe123!') assigns the same known password to every employee created via the CSV import flow. Imported accounts start with a publicly known credential, allowing account takeover until the user changes it.

The generated temporary password is placed into a success flash message (messages.success). The messages framework persists this in the session/signed cookie and renders it in the browser, exposing the credential beyond its generation point.
